sections.heading: White vs Pink vs Brown Noise: Which to Use and When
sections.content:
White noise contains equal energy at every frequency across the audible range (20Hz to 20kHz). This energy distribution sounds bright and high-pitched, similar to TV static or air through a vent. Because human hearing is more sensitive to high frequencies, white noise can feel harsh or fatiguing for some people even at moderate volumes.

Pink noise attenuates high frequencies gradually (reducing energy by 3dB per octave as frequency increases). The result sounds fuller and warmer than white noise. Most people find pink noise more comfortable for extended listening than white noise, and some research suggests pink noise may benefit deep sleep stages more than white noise by matching the spectral profile of natural environments more closely.

Brown (Brownian) noise attenuates high frequencies more steeply (6dB per octave), producing the deepest, most bass-heavy noise character. It sounds like distant thunder, strong wind, or ocean waves. Brown noise is the current popular recommendation for focus use, particularly for ADHD, because the low-frequency emphasis may provide regulation without the higher-frequency content that some people find stimulating rather than calming.

The practical choice: if white noise has felt harsh or hasn't worked, try pink first (same mechanism, warmer), then brown (different character, more anchoring). Most people have a preference that becomes clear after testing each for one session.

sections.heading: Why White Noise Stops Working and What to Do About It
sections.content:
White noise works for environmental masking for most people indefinitely because the masking function is mechanical rather than dependent on novelty. If external noise is still the problem, the white noise is still working.

If you feel the white noise has stopped working for sleep, the problem is usually that the external noise problem has changed (different sound sources, seasonal changes) or that the white noise is now covering sleep-appropriate sounds you're missing (specific partner sounds, household sounds that provide comfort). Try reducing the white noise volume before switching types.

For ASMR-adjacent purposes where white noise is used for internal-noise problems (thought loops, anxiety), habituation is real. The brain classifies a constant simple sound as safe background and it stops occupying the monitoring system that keeps thoughts alive. The fix is adding texture or variation: moving from white to pink or brown, or adding a simple layered element like light rain over the noise base.

Switching completely to ASMR trigger content rather than staying with pure noise is worth trying when white noise has stopped addressing internal noise problems. The mechanisms differ, and ASMR's active monitoring-system occupation may work where passive noise masking has lost effectiveness through habituation.

sections.heading: Optimal Volume for White Noise in Different Contexts
sections.content:
For masking external noise during sleep, white noise should be set to approximately 5-10 decibels above the typical level of the external noise you're masking. If traffic noise sits around 45dB in your room, white noise at 50-55dB covers it effectively. This calibration prevents the common mistake of setting white noise louder than necessary, which can cause fatigue and may affect sleep quality in light sleep stages.

The quick field test: set white noise to where you can clearly hear it when you pay attention. Then lower it until it's barely audible when attending and inaudible when not. The lower end of audibility is better than the clearly audible level for sleep use.

For focus work, white noise should sit lower than for sleep masking: you want it to reduce attention-demanding external variation without occupying your own attention. The rule is the same as for ASMR focus use: audible when attending, inaudible when focused on work.

For infant and baby use, the pediatric recommendation is below 50dB at the listening location. This is significantly quieter than many parents set white noise machines, particularly those positioned near a crib. Distance from the machine is the most practical adjustment: positioning a machine 2-3 feet away rather than in the crib or adjacent to it reduces the sound level at the baby's ear substantially.

sections.heading: Choosing a White Noise Machine vs an App vs a Speaker
sections.content:
Dedicated white noise machines have specific advantages: they work without internet, have reliable loop quality (no gaps or compression artifacts), and typically have simple, reliable controls that work in a dark room without looking at a screen. For overnight sleep use in a consistently noisy environment, a dedicated machine removes app, phone, and internet dependencies.

Phone apps are more flexible but introduce dependencies: battery life, internet connectivity for streaming content, and the risk of notification sounds interrupting during sleep. Downloaded app content removes the internet dependency but not the battery dependency. YouTube or Spotify white noise while sleeping requires continuous streaming, which creates data and connectivity risks.

Smart speakers (Echo, Google Home) with white noise skills or routines work well for consistent sleep masking. They have independent power and don't depend on phone battery. The voice-control interface works without looking at any screen. The limitation is that they require internet connectivity for content streaming.

For travel, a white noise app with downloaded content is the most practical solution. Dedicated machines take luggage space. Smart speakers require power outlets and don't handle all hotel room power sockets. A phone with downloaded content and a Bluetooth earbud covers the sleep masking need without any additional hardware.
